summary: Proposes adding Explicit Congestion Notification to IP, so routers can signal congestion by marking packets instead of dropping them. It is an experimental protocol and was replaced by RFC 3168.

eli5.summary: Instead of throwing away packages when a road is crowded, a router can put a note on them saying it is getting busy so senders slow down.

subtitle: Routers signal congestion by marking packets instead of dropping them

tldr.problem: TCP learns about network congestion by detecting dropped packets, which causes buffering delays and hurts interactive applications. Routers could signal congestion more gracefully before queues overflow.
tldr.mechanism: Two bits in the IP header (ECT and CE) let routers mark packets as experiencing congestion. TCP interprets a marked packet the same as a drop, reducing its send window, but the packet still reaches its destination instead of being lost.
tldr.outcome: This proposal was experimental and was replaced by RFC 3168, which standardized ECN for IPv4 and IPv6.

facts.value: 2 bits (bits 6 and 7 of IPv4 TOS octet)

facts.label: ECT bit
facts.value: Bit 6, set by sender to indicate ECN capability

facts.label: CE bit
facts.value: Bit 7, set by router to signal congestion

today: RFC 2481 was experimental. It was replaced by RFC 3168, which standardized ECN for IPv4 and IPv6. ECN is now deployed in modern operating systems and networks, significantly improving performance for interactive applications and video streams.

sections.title: The Problem with Packet Loss
sections.content:
TCP's congestion control works by gradually increasing the amount of data it sends until the network drops a packet. When TCP detects a loss, it cuts its send rate in half and backs off. This strategy assumes the network is a 'black box'—TCP learns what it can handle only by pushing until something breaks.

The problem is that waiting for packet loss causes unnecessary delays. Interactive applications like web browsing or video calls suffer because the sender does not reduce its rate until packets are already lost. Active queue management mechanisms like RED (Random Early Detection) can detect congestion early, before queues overflow and packets are discarded, but without a way to signal this early congestion to the end system, they are limited to packet drops.

Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets routers signal congestion before dropping packets. Instead of loss, routers mark packets with a single bit. TCP sees this mark, interprets it the same as a lost packet, and reduces its send rate—but the packet still arrives, avoiding unnecessary retransmissions.
sections.eli5: Normally TCP is like a driver who only slows down after hitting a wall. ECN is like a traffic light that warns the driver the road ahead is getting busy, so the driver slows down before there is a crash.

sections.title: The ECN Field in IP and TCP
sections.content:
ECN requires two new bits in the IP header, placed in bits 6 and 7 of the IPv4 TOS octet (or the IPv6 Traffic Class field). The ECT bit (ECN-Capable Transport), set to 1, tells routers the sender is willing to handle ECN. The CE bit (Congestion Experienced), set to 1, signals that the packet experienced congestion on its path.

TCP needs two new flags in its header, using reserved bits:

ECN-Echo flag: The receiver sets this flag in acknowledgement packets when it receives a CE-marked packet, telling the sender that congestion was detected.

Congestion Window Reduced (CWR) flag: The sender sets this flag when it reduces its congestion window in response to a CE packet, so the receiver knows the sender has reacted and can stop repeating the ECN-Echo.

When a TCP connection starts, both sides negotiate whether they support ECN. If both are ECN-capable, the sender sets the ECT bit on data packets. Routers that detect congestion may then set the CE bit instead of dropping the packet.
sections.eli5: Two bits are added to IP packets: one says 'I understand this marking system' and one says 'congestion detected here.' TCP gets two new header flags: one to report congestion and one to confirm the sender reacted.

sections.title: Router and TCP Behavior
sections.content:
When a router detects incipient congestion (using mechanisms like RED), it checks the ECT bit of arriving packets. If ECT is set, the router may set the CE bit instead of dropping the packet. The packet continues to its destination, avoiding the latency of retransmission.

When the TCP receiver gets a CE-marked packet, it sets the ECN-Echo flag in the next outgoing acknowledgement. The sender receives this flag, treats it exactly as if a packet were lost, and halves its congestion window. Critically, the sender does not increase its window when responding to an ECN mark—it only reduces, just as it would for a loss.

Critically, TCP reacts to congestion at most once per round-trip time, even if multiple packets are marked. This prevents the sender from over-reacting to multiple marks of the same congestion event.

The CWR flag ensures robustness: after reducing its window, the sender sets CWR on the first data packet it sends. The receiver uses this to know when to stop repeating the ECN-Echo, avoiding endless duplicates.
sections.eli5: The router marks packets instead of dropping them. The receiver reports the mark to the sender. The sender slows down the same way it would after a drop. The receiver stops reporting once the sender confirms it slowed down.

sections.title: Incremental Deployment and Compatibility
sections.content:
ECN cannot roll out instantly everywhere; instead it deploys gradually across routers and end systems. The RFC design accommodates this by making ECN-capable systems identical in behavior to non-ECN systems when congestion is severe.

A router may drop packets from non-ECN-capable flows while marking (not dropping) packets from ECN-capable flows during light congestion. Only if the queue becomes full does the router drop packets, even from ECN-capable flows. This preserves fairness: ECN-capable flows do not get an unfair advantage.

The design also handles encapsulated packets carefully. When a packet is tunneled, the inner and outer IP headers may have different ECT settings. Rules ensure that CE bits set by intermediate routers are propagated to the inner packet when it is de-encapsulated, so the original sender learns of the congestion.

One concern is non-compliance: a sender could lie and set ECT while ignoring CE marks, gaining throughput at others' expense. However, such a sender is no worse than one that disables TCP congestion control entirely, which is already a concern. The ECT bit gives routers a way to distinguish good actors from bad ones, making compliance mechanisms possible.
sections.eli5: Systems roll out support gradually. New systems get better, old systems work fine, and routers treat both fairly. The design even detects when someone is cheating.

sections.title: Changes to TCP and Related Protocols
sections.content:
To deploy ECN, TCP implementations must:

1. Negotiate capability: During the three-way handshake, both sides signal whether they support ECN using the ECN-Echo and CWR flags.

2. Set the ECT bit: Once negotiated, the sender sets ECT on all data packets.

3. Mark packets: The receiver sets ECN-Echo when a CE packet arrives. The sender treats this like a dropped packet: it halves the congestion window and reduces the slow-start threshold.

4. Confirm response: After reducing its window, the sender sets CWR. The receiver sees this and stops setting ECN-Echo until another CE packet arrives.

Pure acknowledgement packets (that do not carry data) are sent with ECT off, since TCP has no mechanism to reduce traffic on the ACK path in response to congestion on that path.

Other transport protocols (UDP, multicast, etc.) could also be made ECN-capable in the future by implementing similar logic.
sections.eli5: When both sides connect, they agree whether to use ECN. The sender then marks data packets and the receiver reports marks. When the sender sees a report, it slows down and confirms it did so.

left.title: Without ECN
left.desc: Router drops the packet. Sender detects loss and retransmits, incurring delay.

right.title: With ECN
right.desc: Router marks the packet with CE. Packet reaches receiver. Sender reduces rate without retransmission.
